title: Lesson 16: Security Review for a Client Engagement: Threat Model, Secrets, and Compliance
description: Running a security review from the first scoping call: building a client-facing threat model, hunting down secrets before the client's security team does, and presenting compliance evidence instead of assurances.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a threat model?
options: The project budget, the delivery schedule, and the written acceptance criteria
The assets, the actors who threaten them, and the trust boundaries
The model, the provider, and the terminal backend in use
The scope, the identified risks, and the rollback plan
questions.explanation: A threat model names what you are protecting, who threatens it, and the lines an actor must cross to reach it. Without that structure every security decision is a guess on the client's behalf.

questions.question: Why does agent security rely on defense in depth rather than one strong control?
options: Because a firewall placed at the network edge stops every realistic agent threat
Because the model's own safety training is sufficient to contain the agent
Because separate profiles sandbox the agent and fully contain its filesystem access
Because no single layer covers every boundary, so one catches what another misses
questions.explanation: Each layer covers a different boundary, so a gap in one is caught by another. A setup with one strong control and five gaps is a gate with an open field around it.

questions.question: How should secrets be handled in a delivery?
options: Stored in environment variables or credential files, scoped to the task, kept out of prompts
Embedded directly in the scripts so that they are always available when the agent runs at night
Written into the operating doc so that the operator knows each value by heart
Shared across every agent in the estate to make rotation simpler for the team
questions.explanation: A credential belongs in an environment variable or credential file, scoped to the narrowest task that needs it. A leaking secret is the highest-severity, lowest-effort failure, so it is the first thing a reviewer checks.
